title: LiC13: When “Know Yourself” Isn’t Enough
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon argues that most leadership development stops at the self (traits, style, authenticity) while real leadership failure happens in context, when leaders misread the situation, their role and the system's reaction. He dramatises this with Ravi, a thoroughly developed and well-reviewed leader who applies empathy and coaching to a regulatory breach, a pricing problem, a cross-country collaboration issue and an outage, each of which needed a different response. The essay diagnoses four gaps: the self bubble, static role assumptions, the system treated as wallpaper, and the WEIRD bias of the underlying psychology. In response it proposes context-toggling built on self-in-role-in-system, using Cynefin domains, Run/Serve/Change work and the Five Estates as lenses. It then sketches a four-stage developmental arc, a four-block curriculum with role experiments and simulators, and warns about misuse such as box-ticking and using the vocabulary to shut people down. The framework is dense with the author's own constructs and little external evidence, but the central argument is clear and the worked example makes it concrete.
points: Typical leadership programmes (personality tools, strengths, emotional intelligence, authenticity) treat context as neutral background, producing leaders with a rich sense of self but no map of situations.
Ravi's failures come from using one toolkit (empathy, coaching, inclusion) on clear, complicated, complex and chaotic problems that each need different responses.
Roles are constructed by many stakeholders and pulled in several directions, so leaders must ask which version of the role the system is calling for.
The proposed spine of self-in-role-in-system translates into three moves: see the domain, situate the role, and select an action pattern that fits context.
The standard of ready for promotion changes to whether someone can read context with nuance and honestly narrate their own misreads.
quotes: Most leadership development over the last few decades has quietly converged on the same centre of gravity: Fix the person and the leadership will follow.
Ravi did that work very well. His self-description was articulate and consistent. What he lacked was not a sense of self, but a map of situations.

So he used the one set of tools he had – empathy, coaching, inclusion – everywhere. From the outside, this looks like incompetence. From the inside, it feels like betrayal: “You told me this was what good leadership looks like. I did it. And now you’re telling me I failed.
Exported into more constrained systems – tightly regulated industries, strongly hierarchical organisations, non-WEIRD cultures – that same psychology can become quietly cruel.
Context-toggling is, at heart, system literacy plus the courage to act appropriately rather than habitually.

If all your programmes do is help people move from Stage 1 to Stage 2 – one default style to several – you will keep producing very nice, very exhausted leaders who misread context in more nuanced ways.

Context doesn’t care how authentic you are. It cares whether you noticed what kind of situation you were in, what role you were actually playing, how the system would react—and whether you were willing and able to toggle accordingly.
